headline: EVs can send power back to the grid via V2G, making electricity cheaper and more reliable
summary: A new pilot program in Massachusetts is testing Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology, allowing EV owners to earn revenue by supplying power to the grid during peak demand events.
details: Electric vehicles (EVs) possess a "superpower": the ability to send energy back to the grid, known as Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology. This creates a revenue stream for drivers and helps stabilize the power supply, potentially making electricity cheaper.

A coalition including Eversource, National Grid, EnergyHub, Sunrun, and The Mobility House is launching a V2G pilot in Massachusetts. Participants will integrate their EVs into the existing ConnectedSolutions program, earning compensation for supplying power during high-demand events like heat waves.

Utilities are increasingly interested in V2G as they face rising electricity demand from data centers and EVs, alongside the challenge of integrating intermittent renewable sources like wind and solar. V2G offers a flexible way to store and deploy energy without extensive new infrastructure.

Experts consider V2G the "cheapest cost of flexible energy storage" for the grid. EV batteries provide a widespread and reliable source of backup energy, often with six times the capacity of a typical residential backup unit, tapped only during peak demand hours.

While not all current EVs are V2G-compatible, more models, such as the Nissan Leaf, are now equipped with the necessary hardware. The cost of bidirectional chargers, crucial for V2G functionality, is also expected to decrease, increasing accessibility.
caption:
